title: A Guy Thing
full_review:
"A Guy Thing" (MGM) is a stale romantic comedy about an anxious groom-to-be whose future marital bliss is shattered when he falls for his fiancee's free-spirited cousin. While director Chris Koch has assembled an attractive young cast, the contrived premise is mired with cliches, never progressing past sophomoric toilet humor and a hackneyed plot.

Paul (Jason Lee) is a sensitive Seattle ad exec, a week removed from marrying his doting bride, Karen (Selma Blair) -- the piece de resistance of his picture-perfect life. Yet despite her beauty and charm, he senses something is missing. That "something" hulas her way into Paul's life on the night of his bachelor party in the person of Becky (Julia Stiles), a tiki dancer with a firecracker smile hired as part of the evening's festivities.

Paul wakes in the morning to find Becky in bed next to him, triggering a chain reaction of lies which snowball into an avalanche of deceptions and comical cover-ups. As mischievous cupid would have it, Paul soon discovers that Becky is Karen's estranged cousin. Predictably, he quickly recognizes in Becky's joie de vivre the missing ingredient he has been searching for -- the antidote to the ennui of his autopilot existence. The comedy of errors is further complicated by Becky's ex-boyfriend, Ray (Lochlyn Munro), a loose cannon suffering from steroid-rage who will stop at nothing in reclaiming her.

Taken as a whole, the film attempts to make a statement about deception and the liberating effect of truth. That being said, much of Paul's fabrications are presented in a lighthearted manner, camouflaging deceit with frat-house humor. While it is revealed that Paul, in fact, never actually slept with Becky, this is more the result of drunken fatigue than any moral misgivings.

Jason Lee brings a genuine likableness to the role of Paul, yet the film suffers from an abysmal lack of originality. Many of the scenes seem rehashed, having been played out countless times in similar films. It may prove difficult for audiences to invest emotion in such characters since the narrative's outcome is evident by the end of the opening credits. Perhaps a more apt title would have been "A Dull Thing."

Due to an implied sexual relation, sporadic crude language, an instance of rough language, marijuana usage and vulgar toilet humor, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
